chunks: "Most motor brushes are made of carbon, in practice a carbon-graphite composite.

Carbon is chosen because graphite is conductive and also a natural solid lubricant: its layered crystal structure slides easily, so it has low friction and leaves a thin lubricating film on the copper commutator.

It's also soft enough not to chew up the commutator, tolerant of a bit of arcing, and slightly resistive, which actually helps commutation by limiting the circulating current in the coil that's being switched.
Carbon-graphite and electrographite, which is graphite baked at very high temperature, are the workhorses for general use, with a contact drop of about a volt per brush.

Metal-graphite brushes mix copper or silver powder into graphite; they have lower resistance and voltage drop and carry more current, so they're used in low-voltage, high-current motors like car starters.

Then in tiny motors, like those in toys, cameras and pagers, you often see precious-metal brushes: thin leaf-spring fingers of silver, gold or palladium alloys, which have very low contact resistance and noise at low current.
The grade is a compromise between conductivity, drop, hardness, friction and wear, and it depends on the current density and speed."
